units.grammar: Countable and uncountable nouns; determiners. Countable nouns have a singular and a plural form: one ticket, three tickets. Some plurals are irregular: man - men, foot - feet. Uncountable nouns have no plural and take a singular verb: The furniture is new. To count them, use a phrase: a piece of advice, two bottles of water.

There aren't ____ tomatoes in the fridge. (some / any) | any
I bought ____ new trainers yesterday. (some / any) | some
How ____ brothers has Laura got? (much / many) | many
Correct it: The informations are useful. | The information is useful.
I've visited ____ countries in Europe. (several / much) | several
There is ____ milk left, so I can't make coffee. (no / any) | no

Don't worry, we've got ____ of time. (plenty / many) | plenty
She doesn't eat ____ meat. (much / many) | much
Two ____ of bread, please. (slice / slices) | slices

units.grammar: -ing forms. Add -ing to the verb: read - reading. Watch the spelling: make - making, swim - swimming. Use the -ing form after verbs of liking and disliking: enjoy, love, like, hate, don't mind, can't stand. Example: I can't stand waiting for buses. Use the -ing form after adjective + preposition: good at, bad at, keen on, interested in, afraid of, tired of. Example: Marta is keen on skating.
existing_questions_sample: My sister enjoys ____ (paint) portraits. | painting
I'm not very good at ____ (swim). | swimming
____ (eat) vegetables is good for you. | Eating
He's afraid ____ flying. (of / at / on) | of

We're keen ____ trying new sports. (in / on / at) | on
She can't stand ____ (get) up early. | getting
Are you interested ____ joining the club? (on / in / of) | in
Correct it: She is good at draw. | She is good at drawing.
____ (learn) a language takes time. | Learning
Dad hates ____ (drive) in the city. | driving
I'm tired of ____ (do) the same thing every day. | doing

units.grammar: Present simple and continuous. Present simple: add -s or -es for he, she, it (she plays, he watches). Use do/does for questions and don't/doesn't for negatives. Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts: The shop opens at nine. Water freezes at zero degrees. Present continuous = am/is/are + -ing. Use it for actions happening now or around now: Be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
vocab: miss an opportunity to do something
win a prize, medal, game or match

units.grammar: Past simple; used to. Regular verbs add -ed in the past simple: walk - walked, stop - stopped, carry - carried. Many common verbs are irregular: go - went, see - saw. Negatives and questions use did/didn't + infinitive: I didn't see him. Did you call her? The verb be uses was/were and no did. Use the past simple for finished actions, often with a time: We moved here in 2019.
existing_questions_sample: We ____ (go) to the beach last weekend. | went

Where ____ you born? (was / were / did) | were

units.grammar: Past simple and continuous. Past continuous = was/were + -ing: I was reading. They weren't listening. Was she sleeping? Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a moment in the past: At eight o'clock I was having breakfast. Use it to describe the background of a story: The sun was shining and people were chatting.
existing_questions_sample: I ____ (have) a shower when the phone rang. | was having
While we were walking home, it ____ (start) to snow. | started
What ____ you doing at ten last night? (was / were / did) | were
Correct it: She was knowing the answer. | She knew the answer.

units.grammar: Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (1). Must, should and ought to never change form and are followed by the infinitive: You must stop. He should rest. We ought to leave. Have to changes like a normal verb: she has to, do you have to?, he doesn't have to. Must and have to mean it is necessary: I have to wear a uniform. You must see a doctor.
existing_questions_sample: You ____ run near the pool. It's dangerous. (mustn't / don't have to) | mustn't
Tomorrow is Sunday, so I ____ get up early. (mustn't / don't have to) | don't have to
She ____ (have to) wear glasses for reading. | has to
Correct it: You should to sleep more. | You should sleep more.
You ____ to apologise to her. (should / ought) | ought
____ he have to work on Saturdays? (Do / Does / Must) | Does

We ____ to book tickets; entry is free. (don't have / mustn't) | don't have

units.grammar: Present perfect and past simple. Present perfect = have/has + past participle: I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten? Use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020): I lost my keys on Monday. Use the present perfect when the time is not said, or when the result matters now: I've lost my keys (I still can't find them).
existing_questions_sample: I ____ (see) that film last week. | saw
Have you ____ been to London? (ever / yet) | ever
She hasn't finished her project ____. (yet / already) | yet
Correct it: I have visited Paris in 2019. | I visited Paris in 2019.
Look! Someone ____ (break) the window. | has broken
We've ____ had lunch, so we're not hungry. (already / yet) | already
____ you do your homework yesterday? (Did / Have) | Did
He's ____ gone out. You missed him by a minute. (just / yet) | just

My cousin ____ (never / try) snowboarding. | has never tried
When ____ you buy those trainers? (did / have) | did
I ____ (not / read) the message yet. | haven't read

units.grammar: Comparative and superlative adjectives. Short adjectives add -er / -est: tall - taller - the tallest. Note the spelling: large - larger, hot - hotter, easy - easier. Longer adjectives use more / the most: more expensive, the most expensive. Irregular forms: good - better - the best; bad - worse - the worst; far - further - the furthest.
existing_questions_sample: This bag is ____ (heavy) than mine. | heavier
It was the ____ (bad) day of my life. | worst
My phone isn't as new ____ yours. (as / than) | as
Correct it: She is more tall than me. | She is taller than me.
Maths is ____ (difficult) than art for me. | more difficult
Who is the ____ (funny) person in your class? | funniest
This hotel is ____ expensive than the other one; it's cheaper. (less / least) | less
Correct it: It's the most big city. | It's the biggest city.
Your English is ____ (good) than last year. | better
August is the ____ (hot) month here. | hottest
Is your brother as old ____ mine? (as / than / that) | as
This is the ____ (interesting) book I've ever read. | most interesting

units.grammar: Future forms; future continuous. Present continuous + a time = fixed arrangements: I'm seeing the dentist at four. Will + infinitive is for predictions, offers and promises: I think robots will do more jobs. I'll carry that for you. Be going to + infinitive is for plans and intentions you already have: We're going to paint my room this weekend. Future continuous = will/won't be + -ing: I'll be travelling. Will you be using the car?
existing_questions_sample: This time next week we ____ (lie) on the beach. | will be lying
That bag looks heavy. I ____ (help) you. | will help
She's ____ to study medicine next year. It's her plan. (going / will) | going
Correct it: I'll be work at six. | I'll be working at six.
We ____ (meet) Sam at 7 pm tonight. It's arranged. | are meeting
I think it ____ rain tomorrow. (will / is) | will

____ you be using the computer this evening? (Will / Are / Do) | Will
Correct it: He's going buy it. | He's going to buy it.
Don't call at eight. We ____ (have) dinner then. | will be having
I promise I ____ (not / tell) anyone. | won't tell
Future continuous: will + ____ + -ing. (be / been / being) | be

units.grammar: Conditional sentences. Zero conditional: if + present, present. Use it for things that are always true: If you heat ice, it melts. Here if can mean when. First conditional: if + present, will/won't + infinitive. Use it for real possibilities in the future: If it rains, we'll stay at home. Second conditional: if + past simple, would/wouldn't + infinitive. Use it for unreal or unlikely situations: If I had a boat, I would sail to Ibiza.
existing_questions_sample: If you mix blue and yellow, you ____ (get) green. | get
If I see Marta, I ____ (tell) her. | will tell
If I ____ (have) more money, I would buy a new laptop. | had
We'll be late ____ we leave now. (if / unless) | unless

units.grammar: Past perfect. Past perfect = had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had left. She hadn't eaten. Had they arrived? Use it for an action that happened before another action or time in the past: When we got to the station, the train had gone. The later action is in the past simple; the earlier one is in the past perfect: I was hungry because I hadn't had breakfast.
existing_questions_sample: When I arrived, the film ____ (already / start). | had already started
She was tired because she ____ (not / sleep) well. | hadn't slept
Past perfect = ____ + past participle. (had / have / was) | had

____ you ever flown before that trip? (Had / Did / Were) | Had

units.grammar: Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (2). Should / shouldn't + infinitive gives advice: You should pack a jumper. You shouldn't carry too much cash. Need to + infinitive means it is important or necessary: You need to book early in summer. Have to + infinitive means it is necessary because of a rule or law: You have to wear a seat belt.
existing_questions_sample: You ____ show your passport at the border. It's the law. (have to / needn't) | have to

Drivers ____ to stop at a red light. (have / should) | have
You ____ take a coat; it's really warm today. (needn't / have to) | needn't

units.grammar: The passive. Passive = the verb be + past participle. Change be to show the tense. Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle: These phones are made in Korea. Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: The bridge was built in 1890. With modal verbs use modal + be + past participle: Helmets must be worn. It can be done.
existing_questions_sample: English ____ (speak) in many countries. | is spoken
This castle ____ (build) in 1450. | was built
The windows ____ (clean) every week. | are cleaned

____ the photos taken by your sister? (Were / Did / Was) | Were

units.grammar: Relative clauses. Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean. They have no commas: The boy who sits next to me is Italian. Use who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession and where for places. In defining clauses you can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was great. You cannot leave it out when it is the subject.
existing_questions_sample: That's the woman ____ teaches us French. (who / which / whose) | who
This is the café ____ we had breakfast. (which / where / who) | where
I know a girl ____ dad is a pilot. (who / whose / which) | whose
The laptop ____ I bought is very fast. (which / who / where) | which
Correct it: Leo, that is ten, sings. | Leo, who is ten, sings.
Can we leave out 'that'? 'The cake that I made was nice.' (yes / no) | yes
Can we leave out 'who'? 'The man who called was angry.' (yes / no) | no
Madrid, ____ is the capital, is in the centre. (which / that / where) | which

He's the player ____ scored the goal. (who / which / where) | who
Sara, ____ brother is in my class, lives nearby. (whose / who / which) | whose
The village ____ I grew up is tiny. (where / which / that) | where

units.unit_title: Articles: a/an, the and zero article
units.grammar: Articles: a/an, the and zero article. Use a/an with a singular countable noun when you mention it for the first time or say someone's job: I saw a fox. She's an engineer. Use the when you mention something again, when there is only one, or when it is clear which one you mean: The fox ran away. The moon is bright. Use the with superlatives and with seas, rivers, mountain ranges and plural country names: the best, the Atlantic, the Alps, the Netherlands.

I've got ____ idea! (a / an / the) | an

units.grammar: Reported speech. When the reporting verb is past (said, told), the tense usually moves back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, past simple and present perfect to past perfect, will to would, can to could. Could, would, should and might do not change. Pronouns and possessives often change: 'I like my job' - She said she liked her job.
existing_questions_sample: 'I'm hungry.' He said he ____ hungry. | was
'I work in a bank.' She said she ____ in a bank. | worked

'I'm watching TV.' Eva said she ____ TV. | was watching

'We have finished.' They said they ____ finished. | had

units.grammar: Reported questions. Reported questions use statement word order (subject before verb) and no question mark: 'Where is the bank?' - He asked where the bank was. Tenses move back as in reported statements: 'What are you doing?' - She asked what I was doing. Do, does and did disappear: 'Where do you live?' - She asked where I lived. For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you ready?' - She asked if I was ready.
existing_questions_sample: 'Where do you live?' She asked me where I ____. | lived
'Are you tired?' He asked ____ I was tired. (if / that / what) | if
Correct it: He asked where was Tom. | He asked where Tom was.
'What time is it?' She asked what time it ____. | was
'Can you drive?' He asked me whether I ____ drive. | could
'Do you like jazz?' She asked if I ____ jazz. | liked
Correct it: They asked what did I want. | They asked what I wanted.
'Why are you laughing?' He asked why I ____ laughing. | was
'Will you come?' She asked if I ____ come. | would
'Is this your pen?' He asked if it was ____ pen. (my / your) | my
Do reported questions end with a question mark? (yes / no) | no
'Have you eaten?' Mum asked if I ____ eaten. | had

units.grammar: have something done. Form: have + object + past participle: I have my eyes tested every year. Use it when another person, usually a professional, does a job for you: We had the car repaired (= a mechanic repaired it). Compare: I cut my hair (I did it myself) and I had my hair cut (someone else did it).

units.grammar: Different types of clause. Contrast: although, whereas and while join two ideas that are different or surprising: Although it was cold, we swam. I love football, whereas my sister prefers tennis. Although and whereas can go at the start or in the middle; while (for contrast) usually starts the sentence: While I like the city, I wouldn't live there.
existing_questions_sample: ____ it was raining, we went for a walk. (Although / Because / So that) | Although
I study hard ____ I can get into university. (so that / in order to) | so that
She went to London in order ____ improve her English. (to / that / for) | to

units.grammar: Verbs with two objects. Some verbs can have two objects: a direct object (usually a thing) and an indirect object (usually a person): Dad gave me a watch. Pattern 1: verb + person + thing, with no preposition: She sent her friend a postcard. Pattern 2: verb + thing + to/for + person: She sent a postcard to her friend.
existing_questions_sample: I lent my bike ____ Pablo. (to / for) | to
Mum made a cake ____ me. (to / for) | for
Correct it: She gave to me a present. | She gave me a present.
Rewrite without 'to': He sent a text to Ana. | He sent Ana a text.
Rewrite with 'to': I showed Sam the photo. | I showed the photo to Sam.
He bought some flowers ____ his girlfriend. (to / for) | for
Can you pass the salt ____ me? (to / for) | to
Correct it: I told to him the truth. | I told him the truth.
Rewrite with 'for': Dad cooked us dinner. | Dad cooked dinner for us.
In 'Lisa wrote Tom a letter', the indirect object is ____. | Tom
The teacher taught English ____ the children. (to / for) | to
Put in order: me / she / a drink / offered | She offered me a drink.
